title: Basic Web Hacking
description: How a modern web app is built, manual inspection, and your first bug.

1.title: Anatomy of a web application
1.body:
## The three layers of any website

- **Frontend** (YOUR browser): HTML for structure, CSS for style, JavaScript for behavior.
  All of that code is ON YOUR MACHINE — you can read it, modify it and disable it.
- **Backend** (the server): receives requests, queries the DB, makes decisions. You CAN'T
  read its code… you can only infer it from how it responds.
- **Database**: where the data lives (users, orders…).

## The web hacker's tool #1: DevTools

On any page: `F12` (or Ctrl+Shift+I).

- **Elements**: the live HTML — this is where forgotten comments show up
  (`<!-- TODO: quitar admin.php -->`) and sometimes… flags.
- **Network**: every request and response (XHR/fetch included).
- **Console**: run JavaScript on the page; the developer's error
  messages give away internal routes and variables.

Try it NOW on any website: right-click → "View page source"
(Ctrl+U) and search for `TODO`, `password` or `secret`. That habit will stay with you
for your whole career.

## The change of mindset

A regular user SEES a website. A web hacker sees: forms I can tamper with,
URL parameters the server might not validate, JS code that reveals internal
endpoints (`/api/admin/users`), cookies I can read… Everything that reaches your
browser is YOURS to inspect.

web-hacking-basico-t01-q01.prompt: Where does a website's frontend JavaScript run?
web-hacking-basico-t01-q01.hint: Open DevTools: that Scripts tab runs on YOUR machine.

options.a: On the web server, before the page is sent

2.title: Your first bug
2.body:
## The bug that never dies

A real scenario: a form tells you "price: 10€", with JavaScript that stops you from
changing it. The attacker:

1. Opens DevTools → Network.
2. Submits the form normally.
3. Right-clicks the request → "Copy as fetch" — and EDITS the body:
   `precio=1` (or even `precio=-100`!).
4. Pastes it into the Console and hits Enter.

If the server does NOT revalidate, they just bought it for 1€. The rule that follows (and that
you'll see in OWASP): **every security validation must be repeated on the server**.
Whatever runs on the client, the attacker controls.

## Discovering what they don't show you

Beyond the visible form, every website has unlinked routes:
`/admin`, `/backup.zip`, `/.git/config`…

```bash
# Directory fuzzing with ffuf (classic wordlist):
ffuf -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt -u http://LAB/FUZZ
# gobuster dir -u http://LAB -w common.txt   (alternative)
```

The `FUZZ` placeholder is replaced by each word in the wordlist: routes that
exist respond differently (200/301/403) from those that don't (404). This technique, combined
with what you learned about robots.txt in the web-recon-1 lab, is the basic "content discovery"
of every web engagement.

web-hacking-basico-t02-q01.prompt: Why is relying on validation done ONLY with JavaScript in the browser a security flaw?
web-hacking-basico-t02-q01.hint: Who controls what runs in your browser?

options.b: The attacker controls their own browser: they can disable it or send the tampered request straight to the server
options.c: Because it doesn't work on mobile
options.d: It isn't a flaw if there's HTTPS

web-hacking-basico-t02-q02.prompt: In ffuf, which keyword (placeholder) in the URL gets replaced by each wordlist entry?
web-hacking-basico-t02-q02.hint: It's in uppercase at the end of the example URL: http://LAB/____

3.title: Burp Suite
3.body:
## The proxy that sees everything

Burp Suite (the Community edition is enough to learn) sits IN THE MIDDLE:

```text
Browser ──► Burp (127.0.0.1:8080) ──► Server
```

Configure the browser's proxy (or use FoxyProxy) and from then on:

- **Proxy > Intercept**: freezes every request. Edit it (change the price, the
  parameter, the cookie) and Forward. You no longer need "copy as fetch": full control.
- **HTTP History**: everything that has gone through, ready to replay (Repeater).
- **Repeater**: sends ONE request N times with tweaks — the web hacker's workshop.

## The rest of the arsenal (you'll use it in the Jr Pentester path)

- **Intruder**: automates lists (users, IDs, payloads) against a parameter.
- **Decoder**: base64/hex/URL in an instant.
- **Comparer**: diffs two responses (how does the admin's differ from the user's?).

With DevTools you LOOK; with Burp you TOUCH. In Jr Penetration Tester you'll master it (the
Burp Suite module) and in Web Application Pentesting you'll attack vulnerable labs with it
(SQLi, XSS…) — this foundation is enough to start playing in the CyberArena labs
today.

web-hacking-basico-t03-q01.prompt: What is the Burp mode that pauses every request so you can edit it before it is sent called?

web-hacking-basico-t03-q02.prompt: Which Burp module automates attacks with lists of values on a parameter (the brute-force artillery)?

web-hacking-basico-t03-q03.prompt: Burp acts as a proxy between your browser and the server. What advantage does it give you over DevTools?

options.b: It lets you INTERCEPT and MODIFY requests and responses before they arrive (both ways)
options.c: Wait, can DevTools modify them too?
options.d: None: they do the same thing

4.title: Lab: discover hidden content
4.body:
## Practice: content discovery against the lab

```bash
# Fuzzing with gobuster:
gobuster dir -u http://127.0.0.1:18089 -w /usr/share/wordlists/dirb/common.txt

# Or by hand (robots.txt already gives you clues):
curl http://127.0.0.1:18089/robots.txt
# Disallow: /admin
# Disallow: /backup
# Disallow: /dev
```

```bash
# Follow the /dev redirect:
curl -L http://127.0.0.1:18089/dev
```

robots.txt, directory listing and redirects are the three techniques you've just practiced
against a real server. In a pentest, this discovery takes 30 seconds and can
reveal admin panels, backups and development environments.

web-hacking-basico-t04-q01.prompt: Find the admin panel (200 on /admin). Submit its flag.

web-hacking-basico-t04-q03.prompt: /dev redirects (301). Follow it (curl -L). Submit the flag.
